questions.article: Paradise Lies at the Feet of the Mother
questions.q: “Paradise lies at the feet of the mother.” To whom does the article say this saying is chiefly addressed, and why?
options: To mothers – since children follow the path she walks, she should take care that it leads towards Paradise
Yes. It stresses her role in a child’s upbringing.
To fathers – to remind them of their authority
Not quite. The article says: To mothers – since children follow the path she walks, she should take care that it leads towards Paradise.
To rulers – to protect families
Not quite. The article says: To mothers – since children follow the path she walks, she should take care that it leads towards Paradise.
To teachers – to honour their profession
Not quite. The article says: To mothers – since children follow the path she walks, she should take care that it leads towards Paradise.
questions.rationale: “The Hadith about Paradise lying at the feet of a mother is addressed to the mother more than to the children. It emphasizes the importance of the role of a mother in the life of her children.”

questions.q: Scientists say a single message from space would prove intelligence elsewhere. What question does the article put in reply?
options: Who would be able to read such a message?
Not quite. The article says: If one message proves intelligence, does not the library of ordered information in a single cell point to an intelligent source?.
Why has no message yet arrived?
Not quite. The article says: If one message proves intelligence, does not the library of ordered information in a single cell point to an intelligent source?.
How much would the search cost?
Not quite. The article says: If one message proves intelligence, does not the library of ordered information in a single cell point to an intelligent source?.
If one message proves intelligence, does not the library of ordered information in a single cell point to an intelligent source?
Well reasoned. The same standard should apply.
questions.rationale: “‘A single message from outer space would prove there was intelligent life on other planets,’ but an entire library of information inside the most simple cell doesn’t prove that intelligence put it there?”

questions.q: An Olympic champion knelt and kissed the track after his victory. What does the article see in this impulse?
options: A habit learned from other athletes
Not quite. The article says: The inborn human urge to thank a benefactor – which rightly belongs to God, the true Giver.
The inborn human urge to thank a benefactor – which rightly belongs to God, the true Giver
Right. The test is to direct it to the unseen Creator.
A wish to be photographed
Not quite. The article says: The inborn human urge to thank a benefactor – which rightly belongs to God, the true Giver.
Relief that the race was over
Not quite. The article says: The inborn human urge to thank a benefactor – which rightly belongs to God, the true Giver.
questions.rationale: “This is the urge, in fact, to find God, the creator of man, and bow before Him.”

questions.q: The article says the real choice before us is not between peace and no peace. Between what, then?
options: Peace and prosperity
Not quite. The article says: Peace and annihilation.
Peace and annihilation
Yes. Without peace nothing positive can be achieved.
Peace and justice
Not quite. The article says: Peace and annihilation.
Peace and freedom
Not quite. The article says: Peace and annihilation.
questions.rationale: “The option for us is not between peace and no peace, but, rather, between peace and annihilation.”

questions.q: What does the article identify as the main thing that disturbs nature’s peaceful plan?
options: People becoming excessively materialistic, which leads to the exploitation of nature
Correct. Moderation brings spiritual comfort.
The spread of education
Not quite. The article says: People becoming excessively materialistic, which leads to the exploitation of nature.
The growth of cities
Not quite. The article says: People becoming excessively materialistic, which leads to the exploitation of nature.
Differences of language
Not quite. The article says: People becoming excessively materialistic, which leads to the exploitation of nature.
questions.rationale: “What disturbs the peaceful plan of nature is mainly traceable to the fact that people have become excessively materialistic.”

questions.q: “None of you can become a true believer until he likes for his brother what he likes for himself.” What practical guide does the article draw from this?
options: Help only those who can return the favour
Not quite. The article says: Treat others as you wish to be treated – speak politely, give them their due, keep your promises.
Share all property equally
Not quite. The article says: Treat others as you wish to be treated – speak politely, give them their due, keep your promises.
Treat others as you wish to be treated – speak politely, give them their due, keep your promises
Well read. One’s own feelings are the measure.
Agree with whatever others say
Not quite. The article says: Treat others as you wish to be treated – speak politely, give them their due, keep your promises.
questions.rationale: “It is this sensitivity which compels him to be the type of man he wants others to be in their dealings with him.”

questions.q: At Uhud a rumour spread that the Prophet had been killed. What did Anis ibn Nadhr say?
options: “Then the mission is finished”
Not quite. The article says: “If Muhammad has been killed, his Lord has not been killed”.
“If Muhammad has been killed, his Lord has not been killed”
Yes. Faith rests on God, who does not die.
“Then let us return to our homes”
Not quite. The article says: “If Muhammad has been killed, his Lord has not been killed”.
“Then choose another leader at once”
Not quite. The article says: “If Muhammad has been killed, his Lord has not been killed”.
questions.rationale: “But Anis ibn Nadhr said: ‘If Muhammad has been killed, his Lord has not been killed.’”

questions.article: End of the Age of War
questions.q: What two features of the ancient world, according to the article, made war seem unavoidable to ambitious people?
options: Poor roads and slow ships
Not quite. The article says: Hereditary monarchy and a land-based economy.
Illiteracy and superstition
Not quite. The article says: Hereditary monarchy and a land-based economy.
Hereditary monarchy and a land-based economy
Right. Power and wealth could be gained only by seizing them.
Small populations and harsh climates
Not quite. The article says: Hereditary monarchy and a land-based economy.
questions.rationale: “The first of these was family-based monarchical rule. The second was the agriculture-based or land-based economy.”

questions.article: End of the Age of War
questions.q: What changes does the article say have removed those reasons for war?
options: Stronger weapons and larger armies
Not quite. The article says: Democracy, which opens office through elections, and the Industrial Revolution, which opened countless ways to prosper.
Faster travel and better maps
Not quite. The article says: Democracy, which opens office through elections, and the Industrial Revolution, which opened countless ways to prosper.
Fewer countries and fewer rulers
Not quite. The article says: Democracy, which opens office through elections, and the Industrial Revolution, which opened countless ways to prosper.
Democracy, which opens office through elections, and the Industrial Revolution, which opened countless ways to prosper
Well reasoned. Goals can now be reached peacefully.
questions.rationale: “Political rulers now began being chosen through periodic elections… Because of this revolution, today innumerable new economic means and opportunities have become available.”

questions.q: The Quran compares reliance on anything other than God to a spider’s web. Who, according to the commentary, is truly “learned”?
options: One who has travelled widely
Not quite. The article says: One who can draw a great lesson about reality from such small signs in God’s world.
One who can win any argument
Not quite. The article says: One who can draw a great lesson about reality from such small signs in God’s world.
One who has read the most books
Not quite. The article says: One who can draw a great lesson about reality from such small signs in God’s world.
One who can draw a great lesson about reality from such small signs in God’s world
Exactly. Not merely one expert in books.
questions.rationale: “They are not those who have become expert in bookish discourses, but, rather, individuals who are capable of imbibing the sound advice conveyed through God’s signs.”
